auxiliary_material: Study design is a prospective multicenter cohort of 95 Thai patients with advanced NSCLC receiving ICI (monotherapy or combination). Methods included shotgun metagenomic sequencing of stool and 3-day food records. Specific taxa associated with shortened PFS included Firmicutes unclassified (HR 2.40), Ruminococcaceae family (HR 4.30), Intestinimonas genus (HR 2.61 in monotherapy subset), and Enterobacteriaceae family (HR 3.34 in monotherapy subset). Hyperprogressive disease (HPD) was defined as time to treatment failure < 2 months. Dietary pattern analysis used Diet Quality Index-International (DQI-I) and factor analysis identifying five patterns, with Pattern 3 (fats and dairy) showing a non-significant trend (P=0.07) towards association with HPD.
outline_action: Search clinical trial registries and publication databases specifically for results from NCT04645680 (DIET trial). Look for published protocols or results from other registered dietary intervention trials in cancer immunotherapy that include microbiome sequencing and pre-specified mediation analysis plans. If no intervention trials are found, document the explicit absence of such data in the field based on systematic search, using this study's limitation statement as supporting context for the difficulty of such analyses.
remaining_gap: The supplied material does not contain any report from the DIET trial (NCT04645680). Furthermore, this study is an observational cohort assessing baseline diet, not a dietary intervention trial. Consequently, it does not provide evidence of microbiome changes *caused by a dietary intervention* that statistically mediate ICI efficacy. The explicit statement regarding the inability to perform mediation analysis applies to this observational study, not the DIET trial or other intervention studies requested in the gap.
useful_material: This study explicitly states in the Discussion section that 'Subsequent mediation analysis on gut microbiome was not able to be performed' due to limitations including small sample size for dietary data (N=34). It reports observational associations between baseline dietary patterns (specifically high fat and dairy intake) and gut microbiome composition (e.g., Firmicutes unclassified, Ruminococcaceae, Intestinimonas, Enterobacteriaceae) with ICI clinical outcomes (PFS, HPD status) in NSCLC patients. The authors note that while dietary patterns were associated with HPD, the sample size prevented statistical significance for diet-outcome links and precluded mediation modeling.
